Skipp Townsend, Who Was Just Arrested for Murder Conspiracy, Tell His Life Story (Flashback)
recentItems.description: Skipp Townsend, a former member of the Rolling 20s Bloods, recounts his tumultuous upbringing in various LA neighborhoods, marked by gang violence and narcotics trafficking. He describes his transition from petty crimes to dealing, which escalated into a life of danger and incarceration. Townsend highlights his involvement in community programs like Jim Brown's American and Unity One, aimed at reducing gang violence through dialogue. He also reflects on the impact of Nipsey Hussle's death and the broader systemic issues affecting inner-city communities, emphasizing the need for education and job training over incarceration. The discussion highlights the impact of Nipsey's community building and the subsequent gang truce in 2019. Skipp also reflects on the challenges of managing federal funds and the complexities of gang dynamics. The conversation touches on the justice system's flaws, personal stories of loss, and the potential for gang names to evolve while maintaining their essence.

--------
In this VladTV interview, Lil Jungle Boy, also known as George Pollard Jr., recounts the two years he spent in county jail while fighting charges tied to a police shootout, DNA evidence and drug allegations. He describes being placed in K12 protective custody after officials said law enforcement ties in his family raised security concerns, then being moved into a single cell in L.A. County’s Twin Towers jail. According to him, an inmate entered his cell while he was asleep and attacked him with a blade, leaving severe head wounds that required staples and blood transfusions at General Hospital. Lil Jungle Boy says he fought back in self-defense and broke the attacker’s neck. He also alleges abuse involving sheriff’s deputies and a family member in the department. The conversation ends with his no contest plea, a 14-year sentence at 85%, and the fallout from violence behind bars.

--------
Tarso “Tito” Dominguez sits down with VladTV to trace the road from a Cuban exile childhood to the world of 1980s cocaine trafficking tied to Pablo Escobar and the Medellín cartel. Born in Havana and raised between Miami and Haiti, Dominguez recalls his family losing sugar mills after Cuba’s communist takeover, his father’s death from cancer, and a failed $14 million financing push to finish a Haiti sugar mill project. The turning point, he says, came after a lender named Ruben allegedly took a $100,000 escrow deposit tied to the deal. Rather than wait on the justice system, Dominguez describes luring the man with a fake Texas investor pitch, taking him to a farm connected to marijuana smugglers, and forcing repayment through cars, Rolexes, and a Cayman bank connection. An unfiltered look at money, crime, Florida smuggling routes, and the choices that changed his life.

Charleston White joins VladTV to break down the latest developments in the Yella Beezy case connected to the 2020 murder of Dallas rapper Mo3. Speaking with DJ Vlad, White explains why he believes Beezy has a strong chance of being acquitted, pointing to recanted statements, a witness pleading the Fifth, and what he sees as a less confident prosecution compared to the Kewon White trial.  

The conversation covers the alleged role of a woman tied to Mo3, claims involving her child’s father, the freeway shooting that killed Mo3, and how the defense may argue that multiple people had motives. White also discusses Dallas, Texas jury dynamics, celebrity influence, the detective expected to be a key witness, and references to Boosie Badazz being shot in Dallas after Mo3’s memorial.  

A detailed look at one of hip-hop’s most closely watched murder trials.

--------
In this VladTV interview, Rene “Boxer” Enriquez reflects on entering county jail as a teenager and learning the strict rules tied to La Cosa, the Mexican Mafia’s prison infrastructure. Enriquez explains how old street rivalries were put aside behind bars, even when he encountered someone connected to a shooting at his home, because gang violence required permission from higher-ranking figures.

He also opens up about starting heroin at 16, becoming addicted, and selling dope to support his own habit. Enriquez describes withdrawal, hustling for money, and the difference between his experience and the extreme stories often told about heroin addiction. The conversation also touches on Donald Goines’ graphic novel *Dopefiend*, detoxing in county jail, and how later withdrawals in Pelican Bay were far worse due to widespread heroin access in prison. A raw look at addiction, gang politics, and survival inside California’s prison system.
